notes: Only the English pages carry front matter links and AI briefs (ai: see src/ai/BRIEFS.md); a French or Portuguese page with the same slug inherits them, and translationOf names the English page. A brief is used by the AI only when its status is reviewed.

sections.heading: Downloading data
sections.text:
Once login, metadata retrieval, and mapping are complete, the extractor can begin data download.
Instead of relying on a single large DHIS2 request, the extractor is designed to handle extraction in smaller and more manageable batches.
This approach lowers the risk of timeouts for large download requests, thus reducing the chances of incomplete downloads.

Large extractions still need planning:

- Even with caching and chunked processing, very large downloads may take time depending on server performance, user permissions, internet stability, and the size of the requested organization unit and period ranges.

sections.heading: Go to the Downloads Manager and click + New Download Task
sections.text: Downloads Manager with the New Download Task button

sections.heading: Configure the download parameters
sections.text:
Select the name of the mapping (in case you have multiple mappings), the period (start and end dates), and the admin level, then click Start Download.

Configure Download Task dialog

Countdown download configuration:

- Date Range: use the last five years (for example, January 1st 2020 to December 31st 2025).
- Admin Level: use Level 3.

Caching is not only useful for metadata. It also helps the extractor preserve progress and reduce unnecessary repeated work where extraction tasks are interrupted or revisited.

This improves reliability in practical field conditions, especially when:

- internet connectivity is unstable,
- DHIS2 response times vary,
- analysts need to rerun the same extract after refining mappings,
- teams want a reproducible process with less manual repetition.

Tip: If you are testing mappings, validate the metadata and structure first using a smaller extraction range before launching a full national, multi-year download.

sections.heading: Open the CD2030 DHIS2 Data Extractor
sections.text:
The first step is to connect the application to the relevant DHIS2 server. Users provide the DHIS2 instance URL together with their username and password.
Once authenticated, the extractor can read only the metadata and data that the logged-in user is already authorized to access in that DHIS2 environment.

DHIS2 login screen of the Data Extractor

Important: Access rights are controlled by DHIS2, not by the extractor. If a user cannot see a dataset, organization unit, or indicator in DHIS2, the extractor will not bypass those permissions.

sections.heading: Enter valid login credentials
sections.text:
- Start by typing the first three letters of your country. If the URL is indexed, it will pop up and you can select it. If your country's DHIS2 instance URL is not shown, type it in full.
- Then enter your DHIS2 Username and password and click Login.

Server URL suggestions on the login screen

Tip: Start by confirming the DHIS2 base URL before entering credentials. A correct URL prevents login failures caused by pointing to the wrong server environment.

sections.heading: Cache metadata
sections.text:
Done automatically following a successful login, this loads and locally caches the metadata needed for mapping and extraction.
After login, the extractor retrieves the metadata needed to understand the structure of the DHIS2 instance.
This can include items such as organization units, data elements, indicators, category option combinations, datasets, and other configuration objects required for mapping and extraction.

Data Extractor dashboard after login

If you think the DHIS2 data might have changed since the last session, click Sync Meta to ensure the metadata is updated.

Why caching helps:

- Metadata caching reduces repeated calls to DHIS2, speeds up setup for later runs, and creates a smaller download footprint because the extractor only needs to refresh what is necessary.
- Rather than downloading the same metadata repeatedly for every step, the extractor caches it locally for reuse during the session and in later work where appropriate.

sections.heading: CD2030 DHIS2 Data Extractor
sections.text:
The CD2030 DHIS2 Data Extractor helps teams connect to DHIS2, prepare metadata, map indicators, and download routine data in a way that is more stable and easier to reproduce than manual extraction.

It is designed to support large, multi-period downloads while reducing server strain, avoiding unnecessary repeat requests, and preserving progress through local caching.

Access disclaimer: The CD2030 DHIS2 Data Extractor does not allow unauthorized access to DHIS2 data.

sections.heading: What the extractor does
sections.text:
The extractor supports a practical end-to-end workflow:

This process helps analysts produce a cleaner and more reproducible starting point for downstream analysis in DataSuite.

sections.heading: Log in to DHIS2
sections.text: Connect to the correct DHIS2 instance using your server URL and valid account credentials.

sections.heading: Cache metadata
sections.text: Temporarily cache (store) metadata locally for fast access and efficient downloading.

sections.heading: Choose a mapping mode
sections.text: Use Countdown mapping for the harmonized MNCH template or Custom mapping for other programs.

sections.heading: Download data
sections.text: Run extraction with smaller requests and reuse cached metadata to minimize repeat downloads.

sections.heading: Mapping configuration
sections.text:
Mapping defines what data to extract from DHIS2 and how it is structured for analysis.
It is the core step in the Data Extractor workflow in that it fetches indicators of interest,
maps them to the corresponding DHIS2 data sources, and standardizes outputs for DataSuite apps and other analyses.

sections.heading: Navigating the CD2030 DHIS2 Data Extractor
sections.text: Once successfully logged in, the following views help in navigating the CD2030 DHIS2 Data Extractor.

sections.heading: Dashboard
sections.text: Data Extractor dashboard

sections.heading: Mappings Manager
sections.text:
Mappings Manager listing saved mappings

The Mappings Manager is the central place to:

- View all saved mappings
- Search mappings by name or ID
- Create a new mapping

sections.heading: Key actions
sections.text:
- New Mapping: start a new configuration
- Search bar: locate existing mappings
- Actions column: edit, download, clone, or delete the selected mapping

sections.heading: Downloads Manager
sections.text:
Downloads Manager showing a download in progress

The Downloads Manager is where you create download tasks and follow their progress (see downloading data).

sections.heading: Click New Mapping
sections.text: New mapping screen in draft mode

sections.heading: Configure the mapping
sections.text:
Define the mapping name, description, and mapping mode.

Important: Use a clear naming convention. For example:

- Mapping name: CAM2026_CountryName
- Description: MNH Indicators for CAM 2026 Workshop

sections.heading: Select the mapping mode
sections.text: Choose Countdown or Custom in the Mapping Mode field. Both modes are described below.

sections.heading: Mapping modes
sections.text:
Mapping is the stage where DHIS2 source metadata is linked to the structure needed for downstream analysis.
The extractor supports two mapping approaches depending on the use case.

sections.heading: Countdown option
sections.text:
The Countdown option maps indicators and related metadata to the Countdown harmonized MNCH data template.
This is the preferred approach when teams are preparing data for Countdown to 2030 workflows and want a standardized structure that aligns with the embedded resource template used by the application.

This option is useful when:

- the analysis is focused on harmonized MNCH indicators,
- teams want consistency across countries or time periods,
- outputs are intended for Countdown-aligned analytical workflows.

Recommended for standardization: Use the Countdown option when your goal is to produce data aligned with the harmonized MNCH template embedded in the extractor resources.

sections.heading: Custom option
sections.text:
The Custom option allows users to create mappings for other programs or use cases that do not fit the Countdown harmonized template. This gives teams flexibility to work with country-specific program structures, additional service areas, or bespoke indicator sets.

This option is useful when:

- the program area goes beyond the Countdown MNCH scope,
- users need a country-defined mapping structure,
- the extraction supports another analytical workflow outside the standard harmonized template.

Flexible mapping: Choose the Custom option when you need to prepare data for other health programs, local reporting needs, or non-Countdown analytical pipelines.

Mapping summary

There are currently two mapping modes:

- Countdown: this mode has a predefined list of MNCH indicators and structure, as in the harmonized data template.
- Custom: fully user-defined configuration, where the user can download any data that they have access rights to.

Changing the mapping mode midway will reset your progress if the mapping is not saved. Always save your mapping before switching mapping modes.

sections.heading: Indicators configuration
sections.text:
The Indicators Configuration panel is where the indicators of a mapping are defined. Each indicator block has an Internal Name and a Target Export Code, and is linked to the DHIS2 data elements, indicators, or datasets that feed it (Source Configuration). Click Save Mapping to store your changes.

In Countdown mode, the indicators follow the harmonized MNCH template and are marked COUNTDOWN. Search and add the DHIS2 sources for each indicator.

Indicators Configuration in Countdown mode

In Custom mode, you define the indicators yourself, add the DHIS2 sources, and choose which category option combinations (disaggregations) to include.

Indicators Configuration in Custom mode with a data element source and its disaggregation

sections.text:
The CD2030 DataSuite includes a set of integrated applications designed to support the analysis of routine health facility data.
Each app plays a specific role within the analytical workflow, from data extraction to analysis and reporting.

sections.heading: CD2030 Data Extractor
sections.text:
The Data Extractor connects to DHIS2 systems and allows users to extract and map routine health facility data into standardized formats for analysis.

Go to Data Extractor →

sections.heading: RMNCAH App
sections.text:
The RMNCAH App supports analysis across reproductive, maternal, newborn, child, and adolescent health indicators, applying the standardized CD2030 analytical approach. It covers data quality, denominators, coverage, equity and sub-national analysis, and adds Bayesian analysis, continuum of care, family planning, mortality, service utilization and health system pages.

Go to RMNCAH App →

sections.heading: Vaxx App
sections.text:
The Vaxx App focuses on immunization. It follows the same analytical stages as the RMNCAH App (data quality, adjustment, denominators, coverage, inequality and targets, national and sub-national) for immunization indicators.

Go to Vaxx App →

sections.heading: Pooled App
sections.text:
The Pooled App is used for regional and multi-country analysis. It loads the caches saved by the RMNCAH and Vaxx apps from a folder, lets you choose the domain (RMNCAH or Immunization), processes the selected dataset and exports the pooled result as CSV or Excel.

Go to Pooled App →

sections.heading: Exporting results
sections.text: Pooled can export a single table as CSV or Excel, or a selected piece of the pooled file in several formats. Values that are missing are written as empty cells.

sections.heading: Quick downloads of one table
sections.text:
- On a dataset page, use Download and choose CSV file or Excel file. The export is the table for the tab you are viewing, with the Countries and Years filters applied.
- On All datasets, the CSV and Excel buttons export the table currently selected in the list, also filtered.

Format | File name | Contents
CSV | the table name and date, for example

Coverage_-_National_2026-01-31.csv | One table, header row, one row per country, year and area
Excel | pooled_rmncah_2026-01-31.xlsx | One sheet named after the table

sections.heading: Extract a piece
sections.text:
Use Extract a piece when you need several tables, or only part of them. The chips at the top choose Datasets, Countries and Years; choosing nothing means all. Under Columns, keep All columns or choose the columns per dataset: country, year and area columns are always kept. The Preview shows up to six rows per dataset.

The Get the piece card counts datasets, countries, years and rows, then offers three formats:

Format | Result
CSV | One CSV for one dataset, or a

.zip

with one CSV per dataset for several
Excel | One workbook with one sheet per dataset
Pooled file | A smaller

.rds

you can reopen in Pooled

Files are named with the domain and date, for example pooled_rmncah_2026-01-31_piece.zip or _piece.xlsx. Sheet names are limited to 31 characters and the characters not allowed in Excel sheet names are replaced by spaces. Excel sheets have a bold header row, a frozen first row and automatic column widths. Explore this piece opens the result in the app. Start again resets all filters and columns.

Excel and CSV files do not contain the build log. To keep the list of countries, the files that were left out and the log, keep the pooled .rds from Build pooled file.

sections.heading: What is inside the pooled file
sections.text: The .rds is a plain R list, not a country cache. It holds domain, the creation time, the app version, a table of countries (country, ISO3, source file, warning), a table of left_out files with reasons, datasets (one table per dataset) and a time-stamped log. Tables are ordered as in the app's dataset list: Parameters and score, Indicator coverage, Coverage, Mortality, Service utilization, Data quality, Denominators, Estimates and surveys, Equity, Health systems.

sections.heading: Next steps for analysis
sections.text:
- Read the CSV or Excel file in R, Stata, Python or Excel. country and iso3 identify the country, and coverage columns already share names across countries.
- For a full analysis in R, read the pooled file with readRDS() and work on pooled$datasets.
- Compare your results with the methods in the analytical framework, including national coverage.
- For issues with a single country, return to its cache in the RMNCAH App, fix it, save, and rebuild the pooled file.

sections.heading: Using the DataSuite chat assistant
sections.text:
The Countdown chat instructions apply automatically when Pooled is the active app. The assistant has two tools:

- Look Up cd2030.core Data Reference (cd2030Docs): lists an app's pages, the data each page reads and, where available, the rationale for the numbers. The assistant is told to use it before writing R code.
- Read Countdown Cache (readCd2030Cache): opens an app's .rds cache in the managed R session as .datasuite_cache, always reloading from disk.

These tools are designed for country caches, so they are the right way to ask about a single country's file. The pooled file has a different structure (a list of tables), and this documentation could not confirm that readCd2030Cache opens it. If the assistant cannot, ask it to read the file with readRDS() and analyse datasets directly. See Leveraging AI for analysis and interpretation for good practice.

sections.heading: Pooled App overview
sections.text:
The Pooled App combines the saved datasets of several countries into one file, then lets you explore, compare and export the pooled tables. It is the DataSuite tool for regional and multi-country analysis: instead of opening each country one at a time, you load their saved caches together and work on all of them side by side.

Pooled does not replace the country apps. The RMNCAH App and the Vaxx App are where a country's data is uploaded, checked, adjusted and analysed. Pooled starts from what those apps have already saved.

sections.heading: When to use Pooled
sections.text:
You want to... | Use
Check, adjust and analyse one country's facility data | RMNCAH or Vaxx App
Put several countries side by side (coverage, sources, trends) | Pooled App
Get one table containing all countries for a regional report | Pooled App
Extract only some countries, years or columns for another tool | Pooled App

sections.heading: Requirements
sections.text:
- A set of .rds files, one per country, saved by the RMNCAH or Vaxx App. See Preparing caches.
- All files should belong to the same data domain: RMNCAH or Immunization (VAXX). You choose the domain once, before loading.
- Enough memory: the app accepts up to 2 GB of selected files at a time, and reads them one after another.

Pooled keeps only the analysis tables (coverage, data quality, denominators, surveys and so on). The raw facility-by-month data is left out, which keeps the pooled file small.

sections.heading: How the app is organised
sections.text:
The sidebar has one section, Pooling, with two parts.

Build pooled file is a four-step wizard:

- Choose datasets: the domain, what to include, and the files.
- Loading files: each file is read and reported as loaded, loaded with a warning, or failed.
- Review results: decide what to do about warnings and failures.
- File created: download the pooled .rds or go straight to exploring it.

Explore pooled data opens a pooled file and offers these pages:

Page | What it shows
Open a file | Use the file you just built, or upload one made earlier
Parameters | The settings and survey values each country brings
Overall score | The data quality score of each country
Indicator coverage | Coverage by indicator: national, Admin 1, District
Coverage | Coverage with each country's chosen denominators
Mortality | Facility maternal and newborn deaths (RMNCAH domain)
Service utilization | Outpatient and inpatient use, children under 5 (RMNCAH domain)
Compare countries | Continuum of care, source triangulation, level and change, trends
All datasets | Every table in the file, including those without their own page
Extract a piece | Pull chosen datasets, countries, years and columns into a new file

sections.heading: Preparing caches
sections.text: Pooled reads the caches that the country apps save. A cache is an .rds file that holds a country's dataset together with everything computed on it: adjusted data, coverage, data quality results and the choices made in the analysis. Good pooled results depend on well-prepared caches, so it is worth a few minutes to get them right.

sections.heading: Producing a cache
sections.text:
- Open the RMNCAH App (or the Vaxx App) and upload the country's data. The data usually comes from the Data Extractor.
- Work through the analysis: data quality checks, data preparation and adjustment, and denominator selection. See the analytical framework.
- The app saves the cache as an .rds file. When the country's data was uploaded from a spreadsheet or Stata file, the cache is written next to the source file with the same name and an .rds extension. If that .rds already exists, it is loaded again instead of a new one being created.

Repeat for each country, using the same app and the same domain for all of them.

Complete the adjustment and denominator steps before pooling. A cache that is not adjusted still loads, but Pooled warns that its tables use unadjusted data, and coverage will not be comparable with countries that were adjusted.

sections.heading: What makes a cache loadable
sections.text:
For each file, Pooled opens it as a Countdown cache for the domain you chose and then checks:

- The file can be read by R. A damaged file, or one saved by a newer version of R, is reported as unreadable.
- The cache contains a country name. Files without a country or without adjusted data are reported as "Not a Countdown dataset".
- At least one table can be built. Standard tables that cannot be built produce a warning that lists them.

The country and its ISO3 code come from inside the cache, not from the file name.

sections.heading: Naming and folders
sections.text:
- Only files ending in .rds (any letter case) are used. Other files are listed as skipped.
- Put all the countries you want to pool in one folder. Selecting a folder adds every .rds file inside it.
- Keep a clear name, ideally with the date at the end, for example Kenya_master_adj_dataset_20250918.rds. Pooled reads the last run of eight digits in the name as the file date (year, month, day). If there is none, the file's modified time is used.
- Keep one file per country. If two selected files are for the same country (matched by ISO3 code), Pooled keeps the one with the newer date and leaves the other out, with a reason in the log.
- Remove old versions and unrelated .rds files from the folder, or untick them in step 1.

sections.heading: Compatibility notes
sections.text:
- All caches must be loadable by the version of cd2030.core installed with DataSuite (the Pooled package requires version 1.1.0 or later). Caches carry an internal data version, so if an old file fails to load, open and re-save it in the country app first.
- Countries can have different tables. Data quality or survey tables, for example, may exist for some countries only. Pooled records what each file lacks and flags it in the review step rather than failing.
- If the columns of one table differ between countries in type, they are combined as text and a note is written to the file log.

Next: Using the app.

sections.heading: Using the app
sections.text: This page walks through building a pooled file and exploring it. Make sure your caches are ready first: Preparing caches.

sections.heading: Launch Pooled
sections.text: Start Pooled from the DataSuite apps. When DataSuite starts it with a folder selected, every .rds file in that folder is already added to the file list and a banner shows how many files were pre-loaded. The app opens on Build pooled file. Most Pooled pages and buttons are currently shown in English whatever the language selected.

sections.heading: Choose the datasets (step 1 of 4)
sections.text:
Choose the countries' saved datasets

- Data domain: RMNCAH or Immunization (VAXX). This decides which tables the pooled file contains. With Immunization, the tables that only exist for RMNCAH (mortality and service utilization) are not built.
- What to include: Everything in each dataset adds WUENIC, surveys, denominators, data quality and more. Standard tables only keeps just the tables that Explore has pages for.
- Select files to pick several .rds files at once, or Select a folder to add every .rds file in it. A file with the same name replaces the earlier one in the list.

Each listed file has a tick to include it and a button to remove it. The counter shows the total size against the 2 GB limit. Clear all empties the list. Click Load N files.

sections.heading: Load the files (step 2 of 4)
sections.text:
Loading the selected files

Files are read one at a time and each shows its result as it finishes, with an overall progress bar and four counters: Loaded, Loaded with a warning, Failed, Still to load. You can leave the page open while it runs. Cancel loading returns to step 1; a failed file has a retry option. Then click Review results.

sections.heading: Review and confirm (step 3 of 4)
sections.text:
Review results before combining

The Needs your attention list explains every warning and failure. Typical messages:

Message | Meaning and fix
Not adjusted yet, so its tables use unadjusted data | Finish the adjustment in the country app, save, and reload
N of M standard tables could not be built | The cache lacks some analysis; open it in the country app
Has N of the M tables the loaded files have | Other countries have extra tables this one lacks; usually fine
Another file for the country is newer | Duplicate country; the newer file is used
Not a Countdown dataset | The file has no country or adjusted data; it is not a country cache
Could not read the file | Damaged, or saved by a newer R; re-save it

You can leave a file out. Click Combine N files. If some files are left out, a dialog confirms and notes that they are recorded in the file's log with the reason.

sections.heading: File created (step 4 of 4)
sections.text:
File created, ready to explore or download

The app reports the number of countries and datasets and lists each table with its row count. The file is named pooled_rmncah_ (or pooled_vaccine_) followed by the date, ending in .rds. Use Download .rds to keep it, or Explore this file. Build another file starts again.

The pooled file is built in temporary storage for the session. Download the .rds if you want to open it again later.

sections.heading: Explore pooled data
sections.text:
Open a file on Open a file: use the one just built, or upload a pooled .rds made earlier. Only files made by Build pooled file are accepted; any other .rds is rejected with "This is not a pooled file". After opening, the app jumps to the first page that has data.

Every dataset page has the same layout: a file bar (name, countries, datasets, Change file, Download), Countries and Years filters, tabs for National, Admin 1 and District where the table has them, a summary strip (Rows, Countries, Years, Columns), graphs, and a searchable Data table. The Countries and Years filters are shared by all pages, and choosing none means all.

Pages with numbers also have a Measure filter. Graphs use one line or bar per country, with a fixed colour per country. For Admin 1 and District tables the graphs show the median across areas.

- Parameters: settings and survey values per country, with survey coverage dots, neonatal mortality and survey year.

Parameters page

- Overall score: ranking, and a heatmap of the parts of the score.

Overall score page

- Indicator coverage and Coverage: trend over time, ranking of the latest year, and either spread across districts or a change-since-first-year table.

Coverage page

- Mortality and Service utilization: trend, ranking and change.
- Compare countries: four tabs. Continuum of care is a heatmap of the latest facility coverage from the first antenatal visit to the vaccines. Source triangulation shows facility, survey and WUENIC values for DTP3 and MCV1 with the 90% target line. Level and change plots coverage now against change over the period. Trends over time shows the median and the middle half of countries. It needs the Coverage - National table.

Compare countries page

- All datasets: pick any table from the grouped list and see its data.

sections.heading: Reading the output
sections.text:
Key columns you will see:

Column | Meaning
country

,

iso3 | Country name and ISO3 code, always first
adminlevel_1

,

district | Area, when the table is subnational
year | Reporting year
cov_penta3

,

cov_measles1

, ... | Facility coverage; the same name in every country, whichever denominator the country chose

Coverage indicators are ANC 1st trimester, ANC4+, institutional delivery, C-section, HIV test, institutional live births, PNC within 48h, Penta1, Penta3, Measles 1 and 2, BCG, OPV1-3, syphilis test and IPT2-3 (Admin 1 excludes OPV). The Parameters table holds each country's performance threshold, k-factors, national estimates such as nmr and sbr, survey estimates, survey_year and the chosen denominators. For the meaning of scores, adjustments and denominators, see the framework.

Continue with Exporting results.

Coverage columns such as cov_penta3 have the same name in every country, whichever denominator it chose; the Parameters table holds each country's threshold, k-factors, estimates, survey year and chosen denominators (#reading-the-output)
notCovered: The meaning of scores, adjustments and denominators: the page points to the framework (#reading-the-output)

sections.heading: Advanced analysis
sections.text: Three analyses go beyond the basic coverage charts: Bayesian Analysis, Continuum of Care and FPET FP Projection. They build on the adjusted data and the denominators you selected, so finish Data preparation and Denominators first. Methods: Bayesian modeling approach and National coverage.

sections.heading: Bayesian Analysis
sections.text:
Purpose. Combine survey data and routine facility data into one estimate per year, with a range of uncertainty and a short-term forecast. Surveys are used at their reported level, weighted by how uncertain they are. Routine data contribute only their year-to-year trend, and count for less when the overall data quality score is low.

When to use it. When surveys are old or few and facility data are imperfect, and you need a single defensible trend, for example for a synthesis report.

There are two entries in the Bayesian Analysis group of the sidebar: National Analysis and Sub-National Analysis (regions).

sections.heading: Open Bayesian Analysis
sections.text: Choose National Analysis or Sub-National Analysis.

sections.heading: Pick an indicator tab
sections.text: ANC 4 Visits, ANC 1st Trimester, Institutional Deliveries, Measles 1 or Pentavalent 3. The model is defined for these five indicators.

sections.heading: Read the chart
sections.text:
The title is Bayesian Coverage Model Estimates followed by the indicator, and the source note reads Survey Data & DHIS2 Routine Data. The central line is the best estimate; the band is the uncertainty range. Use Download Plot and Download Data in the toolbar.

Bayesian ANC4 estimates at national level

Bayesian ANC4 estimates by region

How to interpret. A narrow band means the data agree; a wide band means few or conflicting data points. The estimate follows an S-shaped rise typical of coverage. Do not read the model as a replacement for good data: if the routine data quality score is low, the estimate leans on surveys.

sections.heading: Continuum of Care
sections.text:
Purpose. Follow coverage along the care pathway and see where women and children drop out.

Where. National Analysis, Continuum of Care in the sidebar. The page has two cards, both titled National Coverage & Continuum, each with the tabs Maternal Continuum and Child Continuum.

- Top card, continuum profile. National continuum-of-care profile: the latest facility value, the latest survey value and, where relevant, the WUENIC value for each step of the selected pathway, for example ANC 1st Trimester, ANC 4 Visits, Institutional Deliveries and PNC within 48 hours for the maternal continuum, or Pentavalent 3 and Measles 1 for the child continuum.
- Bottom card, continuum heatmap. Subnational continuum heatmap: the same steps for each Admin 1 region. Read across a row to see one region, down a column to see one indicator. Red cells are low coverage, yellow intermediate and green high.

The page can generate the national coverage report with Generate Report.

Continuum of care profile

Maternal continuum heatmap by region

How to interpret. A large gap between first-trimester ANC and ANC 4 suggests weak continuity of care. High ANC but lower institutional deliveries points to barriers to delivery care. A gap between Pentavalent 3 and Measles 1 suggests dropout after the early vaccines. A row with many red cells means broad problems in that region; a column with many red cells shows a national bottleneck. Low values can come from reporting or denominator problems, so check quality before acting.

sections.heading: FPET FP Projection
sections.text:
Purpose. Show family planning trends for currently married women aged 15 to 49, from the Family Planning Estimation Tool (FPET, Track20).

Where. It is the FP Projection tab on National Coverage and on Sub-National Coverage.

The chart title is Family planning among currently married women 15-49 years. It draws two indicators: Prevalence of Modern Methods (mCPR) and Demand Satisfied with a Modern Method. Lines are median estimates and shaded bands are 95% credible intervals. FPET data are built-in reference data for the country and do not come from your facility data.

FPET fits a trend through all available surveys, so a smooth curve does not mean a survey exists for each year.

FPET projection

sections.heading: Common pitfalls
sections.text:
- Using Bayesian estimates without stating that they are modelled. Label them as such in reports.
- Reading the FP Projection as a facility indicator. It is model output.
- Interpreting the continuum heatmap without first checking Data quality for the region.

Coverage methods are in National coverage (/en/docs/framework/5-coverage-estimation/)

sections.heading: Coverage, equity and targets
sections.text: These four pages sit in the National Analysis group of the sidebar: National Coverage, Coverage Target, National Inequality (routine data) and Equity Assessment (survey data). All of them need Data Adjustment to have been run and use the denominators chosen on Denominator Selection. Methods are in National coverage and Equity assessment.

sections.heading: National Coverage
sections.text:
Purpose. Compare facility-based coverage with survey and WUENIC estimates for each indicator.

When to use it. After denominators are chosen, to judge whether facility trends are believable.

sections.heading: Open National Coverage
sections.text: There are no filters. The page uses the national level and the denominators you selected.

sections.heading: Pick an indicator tab
sections.text: Tabs: ANC 4 Visits, Institutional Live Births, Low Birth Weight, Pentavalent 3, Measles 1, FP Projection (see Advanced analysis) and Custom for any other indicator.

sections.heading: Read the chart
sections.text:
The lines are the DHIS2 estimate, the WUENIC estimate and the Survey estimate with its 95% CI, from 2010. The caption names the denominator that was used. Use Download Plot or Download Data in the toolbar.

National coverage

How to interpret. If facility and survey values are close, confidence in the trend is higher. Facility values far above the survey suggest a denominator problem or over-reporting. Values far below suggest incomplete reporting, missing private-sector data or missing outreach. Coverage above 100% is a data quality signal, not good performance.

sections.heading: Coverage Target
sections.text:
Purpose. Show the percentage of regions or districts that reach a coverage target, by year.

Filter. Admin Level (Admin 1 or Admin 2).

Tabs are ANC 4 Visits, Institutional Live Births and Vaccine (BCG, Pentavalent 3, Measles 1 and the dropout rates). The chart title states the rule, for example the percentage of units meeting the target. The thresholds applied to regions and districts are:

Indicator | Rule
ANC4 | Coverage of at least 70%
Institutional live births | Coverage of at least 80%
Vaccines | Coverage of at least 80%
Vaccine dropout | Dropout below 10%

Below the chart a table, Target Rate by Region (Admin 1) or Sub-National with coverage >90% (Admin 2), lists the units that reach the target for the indicator you choose in the This table only control. Its title mentions 90%, but the calculation applies the thresholds above. Higher percentages mean less geographic inequality. The same page for regions and districts is described under Sub-national analysis.

Coverage against targets

sections.heading: National Inequality (routine data)
sections.text:
Purpose. See how much regions differ from the national figure, using facility data.

The card National Inequality has one tab per default indicator (ANC 4 Visits, Institutional Live Births, Low Birth Weight, Pentavalent 3, Measles 1) plus Custom. Each dot is an Admin 1 region; the line is National Coverage. A wide spread of dots means high inequality.

Under it, choose Select Years and a Palette (Greens, Blues, Reds or Purples) for the Sub-National Mapping card, which maps the coverage of each region for the selected years.

National inequality

sections.heading: Equity Assessment (survey data)
sections.text:
Purpose. Show inequality between population groups, using household survey data.

When to use it. When survey files were loaded (or the built-in ones cover your country) and you want to know who is being left behind.

sections.heading: Choose the Equity Type
sections.text: Area (Rural, Urban), Maternal Education (No education, Primary, Secondary or higher) or Wealth Quintile.

sections.heading: Pick an indicator tab
sections.text: ANC 4 Visits, Institutional Live Births, Low Birth Weight, Pentavalent 3, Measles 1 or Custom.

sections.heading: Read the equiplot
sections.text:
Each group has its own line over time, with the national trend for comparison. Generate Report opens the national inequality report.

For wealth, read the pattern: only the richest ahead means top inequality, evenly spaced groups mean linear inequality, and the poorest far behind means bottom inequality (marginalisation). Each calls for a different programme response. Focus on the latest data point, the change since 2010 and whether the gap is closing.

Equity by area of residence

Equity by wealth quintile

Equity by maternal education

sections.heading: Common pitfalls
sections.text:
- Survey points are few and have confidence intervals. Do not over-read small differences.
- Facility inequality between regions can come from denominator or reporting differences, not real differences in access.
- The equity pages rely on the survey files and the survey year from Load Data.

ai.summary: Four National Analysis pages: National Coverage, Coverage Target, National Inequality (routine data) and Equity Assessment (survey data). All need Data Adjustment and use the denominators chosen on Denominator Selection.

The Coverage Target table title mentions 90%, but the calculation applies the thresholds above (#coverage-target)

Methods are in National coverage (/en/docs/framework/5-coverage-estimation/)
Equity methods are in Equity analysis (/en/docs/framework/6-equity-analysis/)

Facility close to survey: more confidence; far above: denominator problem or over-reporting; far below: incomplete reporting, missing private sector or outreach; above 100% is a data quality signal (#read-the-chart)
National Inequality: each dot is an Admin 1 region, the line is national coverage; a wide spread means high inequality (#national-inequality-routine-data)
Equity Assessment: an equiplot per Equity Type (Area, Maternal Education, Wealth Quintile); for wealth, top, linear or bottom inequality each calls for a different response (#read-the-equiplot)
Coverage Target: percentage of units meeting the target; higher means less geographic inequality (#coverage-target)

sections.heading: Data preparation
sections.text: Data preparation turns the reported numbers into an analysis-ready dataset. It has three pages in the Data quality section: Remove Years, Data Adjustment and Data Adjustment Changes. Running the adjustment is what unlocks the Denominators and Analysis pages. The method, formulas and business rules are in Data adjustment.

sections.heading: Remove Years
sections.text:
Purpose. Leave out years whose data cannot be relied on, for example a year with almost no reporting or a system-wide failure.

When to use it. After the data quality pages show a year that is clearly erratic and you have a real-world reason to believe it. If you have no reason, keep the year.

sections.heading: Open Remove Years
sections.text: It is under Data quality in the sidebar.

sections.heading: Select Years to Remove
sections.text: The chips list the years present in the data. Select one or more.

sections.heading: Press Confirm Removal
sections.text:
The message changes from No years have been removed yet to Data for the following years has been removed, followed by the years. To bring a year back, deselect it and confirm again.

Remove years

sections.heading: Data Adjustment
sections.text: Purpose. Correct for incomplete reporting and extreme outliers. Missing and outlier values are replaced using the district median for the same year. Reported counts are then scaled up with a K-factor, which represents the volume of services in non-reporting facilities relative to reporting ones.

sections.heading: Choose the K-Factors
sections.text: The card K-Factors (Adjustment Factors) has four selectors: ANC K-Factor, Delivery K-Factor, Vaccines K-Factor and OPD K-Factor. Each offers 0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75 and 1. A value of 0 assumes that non-reporting facilities delivered no services, 0.25 assumes a quarter of the volume of reporting facilities, and 1 the same volume. Raise a factor when facilities that report poorly, such as private ones, provide a large share of that service.

sections.heading: Press Adjust Data
sections.text: The message goes from Dataset not adjusted to Adjusting ... and then Data Adjusted. Do this even if you keep every factor at 0, because it is what unlocks the analysis pages.

sections.heading: Download the result if you need it
sections.text:
Download Adjusted Dataset saves the adjusted master dataset as a .dta file.

Changing the K-factors or the removed years discards the adjusted dataset. Press Adjust Data again, otherwise the analysis pages will not reflect your change. If the adjustment fails, the message shows the reason.

According to the methodology, no adjustment is applied for districts whose reporting rate is below 75%, because imputation is unreliable there. The methodology flags such years as unreliable for coverage calculations.

K-factor selection

sections.heading: Data Adjustment Changes
sections.text:
Purpose. See what the adjustment did to each indicator.

How to read it. The card Visualize effects of changes has one tab per indicator: Institutional Deliveries, Institutional Live Births, Pentavalent 1, ANC 1 and OPD Under 5 Years, plus a Custom tab for any other indicator. Each chart compares the number of events before and after adjustment for completeness and outliers, by year. Use Download Plot and Download Data on the toolbar. Generate Report opens the adjustment report.

Before and after adjustment

sections.heading: How to interpret the results
sections.text:
- A small gap between the lines means reporting was already nearly complete.
- A wide gap in one year points to a year with low reporting. Report the K-factor used and the percentage change it produced, as the methodology recommends.
- The effect is largest for services with the lowest reporting rates. Compare with the Reporting Rate page.

sections.heading: Common pitfalls
sections.text:
- Removing a year you should keep silently shortens every later trend.
- Using a high K-factor to hide poor reporting hides the problem instead of fixing it. Document your choice.
- Mortality indicators are not adjusted for reporting or outliers, because deaths are few and volatile (see Mortality).

Data Adjustment: choose the K-Factors and press Adjust Data until it says Data Adjusted (#press-adjust-data)

sections.heading: Data quality
sections.text: The Data quality section answers one question before any coverage is calculated: can the facility data be trusted? It contains five pages. Read them in this order, then move on to Data preparation. The method is explained in Data quality assessment.

sections.heading: Open the page from Data quality in the sidebar
sections.text: Load Data must be finished first. These pages do not need Data Adjustment.

sections.heading: Set the filters
sections.text: Most pages have an Indicator chip, an Admin Level chip (Admin 1 or Admin 2) and, when Admin 1 is selected, a region chip with Select All to focus on one region.

sections.heading: Read the chart, then the table below it
sections.text: Charts show the pattern. Tables list the districts and months behind it. Use the toolbar of a card for Download Plot (PNG) and Download Data (Excel), and the This table only year selector for tables.

sections.heading: Reporting Rate
sections.text:
Shows how completely facilities reported, by service, year and area.

- Filters: Indicator (ANC, Institutional Delivery, Vaccination, OPD), Performance Threshold (default 90%; quick picks 70, 80, 90, 95) and Admin Level.
- Sub-National Reporting Rate: tabs Heat Map and Bar Graph show the reporting rate of the selected service by year for each area.
- National Reporting Rate (or District Reporting Rate in a region): the percent of districts whose reporting rate is below the threshold, one panel per service.
- Sub-National Units with Low Reporting: the districts or regions under the threshold for the selected year.

The Performance Threshold you set here is stored in the dataset and reused by the Overall Data Quality Score and the Service Utilization DQA.

Sub-national reporting rate heat map

sections.heading: Outlier Detection
sections.text:
Finds extreme monthly values. A value is an extreme outlier when it lies more than 5 times the median absolute deviation (MAD) away from the monthly median for that year.

- Filters: Indicator and Admin Level.
- Indicators with Outliers: tabs Heat Map, Indicator Bar Graph and Region Bar Graph show the percent of monthly values that are not outliers.
- Sub-National Units with Extreme Outliers: every flagged district and month with the value, median and MAD.
- Sub-National Trends: pick a region and read the month-by-month line against the median and the outlier bounds (plus or minus 5 MAD).

Expect at least 99% of monthly values, and 90% of districts, to be free of extreme outliers. A sudden peak may be a campaign, not an error. Check the trend before you decide.

Outlier detection heat map

sections.heading: Data Missingness
sections.text:
Shows which indicators and areas have missing reports.

- Filters: Indicator (with Select All) and Admin Level.
- Indicators with Missing Data: tabs Heat Map (percent of missing reports by year and area), Complete Indicators (percent of districts with complete data) and Missing Indicators by Region (trend in completeness).
- Sub-National Units with Missing Data: the districts with gaps for the selected indicator and year.

Data missingness heat map

sections.heading: Internal Consistency
sections.text:
Checks that related indicators move together. Two cards are shown.

- Ratio Plots: the yearly ratios ANC1 / Penta1 and Penta1 / Penta3 against the expected ratio. Expected ratios come from the survey coverage values entered in National Rates, so wrong survey values distort this check.
- Consistency Checks: tabs ANC1 and Penta1, Penta1 and Penta3 and Custom Check (choose an X axis and a Y axis). Each dot is a district, shown with a Linear fit and a Diagonal. Dots far from the diagonal deserve a look.

A district counts as consistent when its yearly ratio lies between 1 and 1.5.

Ratio plots

Consistency checks between ANC1 and Penta1

sections.heading: Overall Data Quality Score
sections.text:
One table per year, with a region filter to see a single Admin 1 area.

Block | Rows
1. Completeness | % of expected monthly facility reports (national); % of districts at or above the threshold; % of districts with no missing values for the 4 forms
2. Extreme outliers | % of monthly values that are not extreme outliers; % of districts with no extreme outliers
3. Consistency | Ratios ANC1 / Penta1 and Penta1 / Penta3; % of districts within the expected range

The last row is the Annual data quality score, the mean of the national and district completeness rows (1a, 1b), the two outlier rows (2a, 2b) and the two district consistency rows (3c, 3d). Use Download Plot and Download Data. Generate Report opens the data quality report.

Overall data quality score

sections.heading: Common pitfalls
sections.text:
- A low score is a reason to investigate, not always to discard a year. Compare with local events before using Remove Years.
- Reporting rate measures whether reports arrived, not whether the numbers are right. Use Outlier Detection and Internal Consistency together.
- District results are noisier than regional ones because they rest on smaller numbers.

ai.summary: The five Data quality pages answer whether the facility data can be trusted before any coverage is calculated. Read them in order: Reporting Rate, Outlier Detection, Data Missingness, Internal Consistency, Overall Data Quality Score.

Consistent district: its yearly ratio lies between 1 and 1.5 (#internal-consistency)

Expect at least 99% of monthly values, and 90% of districts, to be free of extreme outliers; a sudden peak may be a campaign, so check the trend (#outlier-detection)
Expected ratios come from the survey values in National Rates, so wrong survey values distort the consistency check (#internal-consistency)
A low score is a reason to investigate, not always to discard a year; reporting rate measures whether reports arrived, not whether the numbers are right (#common-pitfalls)
The method is in Data quality assessment (/en/docs/framework/2-data-quality-assessment/)

Outlier Detection: Indicators with Outliers (Heat Map, Indicator Bar Graph, Region Bar Graph), Sub-National Units with Extreme Outliers, Sub-National Trends (#outlier-detection)

sections.heading: Denominators
sections.text: Coverage is the number of people who received a service divided by the number who needed it. The numerator comes from facility data; the denominator has to be estimated. The Denominators section has two pages, Denominator Assessment and Denominator Selection. Both unlock after Data preparation. The method is described in Denominator assessment and selection.

sections.heading: Denominator options
sections.text:
The UN projection is shown in the comparison charts only. The Maternal denominator and Vaccination denominator selectors offer the other five options.

Option in the app | Meaning
UN | UN projection of live births
DHIS2 | DHIS2 projection of live births
ANC 1 | Derived from women attending a first antenatal visit
Pentavalent 1 | Derived from children receiving the first pentavalent dose
ANC 1 Population Growth | ANC 1 derived, adjusted for annual population growth
Penta 1 population Growth | Penta 1 derived, adjusted for annual population growth

sections.heading: Denominator Assessment
sections.text:
Purpose. Decide which population indicator is consistent between the UN and DHIS2 projections. That choice drives the two population-growth options.

When to use it. First, before Denominator Selection.

sections.heading: Open Denominator Assessment
sections.text: It is the first page of the Denominators section.

sections.heading: Compare the three tabs
sections.text: The card Population Comparison has the tabs Population, Births and Under 1. Each plots the UN projection against the DHIS2 projection in thousands, by year. The Births tab shows DHIS2 live births and DHIS2 total births.

sections.heading: Select Best Population
sections.text:
In the filter bar choose the population source that is most consistent with the UN: Live births (DHIS2), Total births (DHIS2), Total population (DHIS2) or Under 1 year (DHIS2).

Choose a series where the two sources are close and follow the same direction. Large gaps between UN and DHIS2 suggest an outdated census base or a wrong population entry in the workbook.

Population comparison between UN and DHIS2

sections.heading: Denominator Selection
sections.text:
Purpose. Choose the best denominator for vaccination indicators and for maternal indicators.

Filters. Maternal denominator, Vaccination denominator and Admin Level (National, Admin 1 or Admin 2, with a region chip). The two denominator choices are what the rest of the analysis uses. They appear afterwards in the Denominator row of every analysis page.

Three cards support the decision:

sections.heading: Survey comparison (National Coverage)
sections.text: For each indicator tab (Institutional Live Births and Pentavalent 3) the bars show facility-based coverage in the survey year under each denominator, compared with the national survey coverage. If survey estimates are missing the card shows No coverage to show yet and a Go to Load Data button.

sections.heading: Subnational Derived Coverage
sections.text: Compares coverage by region and denominator in the survey year. Look for the option that agrees best with the survey across regions and for implausible values, such as coverage far above 100%.

sections.heading: Population Trend
sections.text:
Shows national coverage over time (or for the selected region) for each denominator. Look for plausible, smooth trends.

Combine the three views, pick one denominator per indicator type and record why in your notes.

Best denominator selection

National coverage over time by denominator

sections.heading: How to interpret the results
sections.text:
- The best denominator is not the one that gives the highest coverage, but the one closest to the survey and stable over time.
- Denominators derived from ANC 1 or Penta 1 assume that most of the population attends the service and that facilities report completely. They are weakest where reporting is poor. Return to Data quality if results look odd.
- DHIS2 projections often drift when they are based on an old census.

The denominator you select changes every coverage, inequality, target, mortality and health system chart. If you change it later, review the pages that depend on it and regenerate any exported figures.

sections.heading: Common pitfalls
sections.text:
- Comparing against the survey when the survey year is far from the analysis years. Weigh that in your judgement.
- Missing survey coverage values in Load Data, which leaves the survey comparison empty.
- Choosing a denominator per chart instead of once for the whole analysis.

Continue with Coverage, equity and targets.

- Sharing a chart without its data or the denominator. Always state the denominator and adjustment used.
- Asking the assistant about results before Data Adjustment has been run and saved in the app.
- Accepting an AI interpretation without checking data quality. The assistant reads the same data, so poor data give poor conclusions.

sections.heading: Getting started
sections.text: This guide takes you from opening the RMNCAH App in DataSuite to a dataset that is ready for analysis. The methodology behind these steps is described in Analysis setup.

sections.heading: Start the app from DataSuite
sections.text:
On the DataSuite welcome page choose Open in RMNCAH (see Navigating the DataSuite interface). The app needs a file to work on, so DataSuite asks you to pick one. Accepted types are .xls, .xlsx, .dta and .rds.

Use the Excel workbook from the Data Extractor the first time, and the saved .rds afterwards.

sections.heading: Check that the file was read
sections.text:
Open Load Data in the sidebar. When DataSuite hands the file to the app, it is read automatically and a green Upload successful banner names the file. If the page shows an Upload HFD data box instead, choose the file there.

Loading routine data

sections.heading: Two ways through Load Data
sections.text:
- A resumed .rds file was already validated. The wizard is replaced by a Ready for analysis page with one row per step (for example 15 of 15 fields set, Using the built-in shapefile) and an Edit link that reopens any step. Continue to analysis takes you to Reporting Rate.
- A new Excel or Stata file goes through the walkthrough below. A step opens only after you press Continue (or Skip to) on the previous one. Steps marked optional can be skipped.

sections.heading: Upload Data
sections.text:
The Dataset card shows the loaded file. Download Master Dataset saves the merged dataset as a .dta file.

The card Additional reference data (optional) lets you replace the built-in country reference sets with your own .dta files: Upload UN Estimates data, Upload WUENIC estimates and Upload UN Mortality estimates. Restore default returns to the built-in data.

sections.heading: Data Quality
sections.text:
The checks run automatically. A banner reads either All checks passed, no blocking issues found or Some checks found issues that need fixing before you can continue.

- Blocking checks: Admin, Population and Service sheets found; country, admin-1 and district columns present; exactly one country, recognised by name; districts match between the Admin sheet and every other sheet; district names consistent across years; no missing months (every district-year has all 12); every month name recognised (English or French).
- Informational checks: estimated live births not lower than facility live births (10% margin), population data not pasted into service data, every indicator has some data, month names labelled consistently across sheets.
- Mapping checks: survey and shapefile region names match your dataset. Mismatches are fixed in the mapping steps.

Fix blocking problems in the workbook and load it again.

sections.heading: Survey Files (optional)
sections.text: Upload up to five .dta files in the Survey data folder card: National data, Regional data, Area data, Maternal education data and Wealth index quintile data. They power equity analysis, survey comparison lines and sub-national comparisons. A file that cannot be read shows Upload failed with the reason.

sections.heading: National Rates
sections.text:
Enter the survey values used to derive denominators. Every field is required and Continue stays disabled while Required fields remaining is shown.

- Survey reference: Recent Survey Year (2015 to 2030) and Survey Data Start Year. Use the two most recent surveys, for example 2018 when surveys exist for 2008, 2013, 2018 and 2023.
- Maternal and newborn: ANC1, ANC4, Institutional Delivery, C-Section and Low Birth Weight coverage as percentages (0 to 100), and Pregnancy Loss, Twin Births, Stillbirth, Neonatal Mortality and Post-Neonatal Mortality as proportions (0 to 0.05, for example 0.03 means 3%).
- Immunization: BCG, Penta1, Penta3 and Measles 1 coverage as percentages.

If you uploaded a national survey file, the values are pre-filled and a banner says so. Check them. The definitions are in the methodology.

National rates for denominator calculation

sections.heading: Shapefile (optional)
sections.text: The app uses a built-in shapefile for the country. To use your own, upload the .shp, .dbf, .shx and .prj files, pick the column that holds the region (admin-1) names and press Use this shapefile.

sections.heading: Map Survey and Map Shapefile
sections.text: When survey or shapefile region names differ from your dataset, press Match Region Names, correct the matches and save. Save at least once, even if nothing needed changing. Clear mapping starts again.

sections.heading: Finish
sections.text:
On the last step press Finish Loading Data. The app merges the sheets, saves a copy named after your file with _rmncah.rds added, in the same folder, and shows Ready for analysis.

When you open the same Excel or Stata file again, the saved _rmncah.rds copy next to it is used instead. Delete that copy if you changed the workbook and want to load it afresh.

sections.heading: RMNCAH App overview
sections.text:
The RMNCAH App within the CD2030 DataSuite is designed to support the analysis of routine health facility data for key RMNCAH indicators.
It provides a standardized framework for transforming raw DHIS2 data into meaningful insights on service coverage, data quality, and equity.

Building on the outputs from the Data Extractor, the RMNCAH App guides users through a structured analytical workflow that includes data validation, adjustment, and indicator computation.
This ensures that analyses are consistent, reproducible, and aligned with the CD2030 methodological approach.

The app enables users to:

- Assess data quality through standardized DQA metrics
- Apply numerator and denominator adjustments
- Generate national and subnational coverage estimates
- Explore inequalities and trends across time and geography
- Produce outputs for reporting, including synthesis reports and visualizations

By integrating methodological rigor with a user-friendly interface, the RMNCAH App facilitates evidence-based decision-making and supports countries in monitoring progress across RMNCAH priorities.

sections.heading: Who uses it
sections.text: The app is written for the country analytical team of a CD2030 review: monitoring and evaluation officers, HMIS and DHIS2 data managers, programme managers for maternal, newborn, child and adolescent health, and the analysts who prepare annual health sector reviews. You do not need to write code. Everything is done through pages, filters, charts and tables. Analysts who prefer scripting can work on the same saved dataset through the DataSuite chat assistant (see Exports, reports and AI).

sections.heading: What you can load
sections.text:
The app opens one dataset at a time. It accepts four file types:

File type | What it is | Typical use
.xlsx

,

.xls | Excel workbook with the sheets Admin_data, Population_data, Reporting_completeness and at least one Service_data sheet, as produced from the

Data Extractor | First load of a country dataset
.dta | Stata file | First load, or a master dataset downloaded earlier
.rds | The saved dataset that the app creates when you finish loading | Resuming work: every loading step is already done

During the load wizard you can also add optional survey files (.dta), a custom shapefile and country-specific UN, WUENIC and UN mortality reference files (.dta). Built-in reference data for the country are used when you add nothing. See Getting started.

sections.heading: How it relates to the Data Extractor and the methodology
sections.text:
- The Data Extractor produces the routine data file. The RMNCAH App starts where the extractor stops.
- The methodology chapters explain why each analysis is done and how to interpret it. Every page guide in this section ends with a link to the matching chapter, and the Get Help button in the app opens the same chapters.

sections.heading: Layout and navigation
sections.text:
RMNCAH App navigation panes

- Sidebar. The pages are grouped in five sections: Start, Data quality, Denominators, Analysis and Output. Change Language at the top switches the app between English, French and Portuguese.
- Locked pages. Pages are greyed out until they can be used. Load Data is always open. The Denominators and Analysis groups and Reports unlock only after you have finished loading a dataset and run Data Adjustment.
- Page header. Each page shows its title and a one-line subtitle. Get Help opens the matching methodology chapter. Pages that feed a standard report also show Generate Report. Analysis pages show a Denominator row that tells you which denominators the numbers were divided by; it is set on the Denominator Selection page.
- Filter bar. Filters appear as chips at the top of a page, for example Indicator, Admin Level, Performance Threshold or Select Years.
- Chart cards. A card usually has one tab per indicator plus a Custom tab where you pick any other analysis indicator. The card toolbar downloads the chart (Download Plot, PNG) or its numbers (Download Data, Excel), and offers tools to edit labels, change the view or style, and expand the chart.
- Tables. A control marked This table only (year or indicator) changes that table alone. Each table has its own Download Data button.

sections.heading: Step-by-step analytical flow
sections.text:
Countdown analysis workflow

The analysis steps page walks through the same sequence and links each step to its methodology chapter.

ai.summary: The RMNCAH App analyses routine health facility data for RMNCAH indicators: it checks data quality, applies numerator and denominator adjustments, estimates national and sub-national coverage, explores inequalities and trends, and produces reports. It starts where the Data Extractor stops and follows the CD2030 methodology; each page guide links to the matching framework chapter.

The workflow and the chapters behind it are in the framework (/en/docs/framework/0-workflow/)

sections.heading: Mortality
sections.text:
The Mortality group looks at deaths recorded in health facilities: institutional maternal mortality, stillbirths and neonatal deaths before discharge. It has three pages: Institutional Mortality, Mortality Mapping and Mortality Completeness. The method, definitions and formulas are in Mortality.

Mortality figures use the reported numbers of deaths without the reporting-rate and outlier adjustment applied to other indicators, because deaths are few and fluctuate. They still depend on the denominator you selected (live births or births). If a value looks like a data entry error, check it in Outlier Detection and treat it with the methodology's guidance.

sections.heading: Institutional Mortality
sections.text:
Purpose. Show the level and trend of institutional mortality and check whether it is plausible.

When to use it. First, to see the rates; then use the second card to test data quality.

sections.heading: Open Institutional Mortality
sections.text: It is under Mortality in the Analysis group.

sections.heading: Read the first card, Institutional Mortality
sections.text: Tabs: Maternal Mortality (per 100,000 live births in facilities), Still Birth Rate and Neonatal Deaths. Dots are regions and the line is the country, by year.

sections.heading: Read the second card, Institutional Mortality DQA
sections.text:
Tabs: Fresh Stillbirths (fresh stillbirths as a percentage of all stillbirths), SBR to Maternal Death Ratio (stillbirths per maternal death) and Neonatal / Maternal Deaths (institutional neonatal deaths per maternal death). Each chart shows the Median and an Expected range, and a note under the chart gives the range: 30 to 55 for fresh stillbirths, 6 to 15 for stillbirths per maternal death and 5 to 10 for neonatal deaths per maternal death.

Institutional maternal mortality by region and year

Fresh stillbirths as a percentage of total stillbirths

How to interpret.

- A very low maternal mortality ratio with a low stillbirth-to-maternal-death ratio can point to under-reporting of deaths, not to good care.
- A share of fresh stillbirths far outside its range suggests that fresh and macerated stillbirths are misclassified.
- Neonatal deaths here are deaths of live-born babies before discharge, so they understate community neonatal mortality.
- Regions that sit outside the range in every year are the priority for data review.

sections.heading: Mortality Mapping
sections.text:
Purpose. Map institutional mortality across regions.

Filters. Select Years (one or several) and Palette (Greens, Blues, Reds or Purples; the default is Reds).

Tabs: Maternal Mortality and Still Birth Rate. Each map shows the values by region for the selected years, which makes geographic clusters visible.

Institutional maternal mortality by region

Pitfall. High values on a map are not always high mortality. Regions with few births can swing widely, and regions that report well can look worse than regions that under-report.

sections.heading: Mortality Completeness
sections.text:
Purpose. Estimate how completely facilities report deaths, by comparing the reported institutional rate with an expected rate built from UN estimates.

When to use it. After the DQA charts, to judge whether reported mortality can be used at all.

Tabs: Institutional MMR and Institutional SBR. Completeness is the reported institutional rate divided by the expected institutional rate, drawn for several assumptions about how much higher community mortality is than institutional mortality and for the lower bound, median and upper bound of the UN estimate. Use Generate Report to open the mortality report.

If external evidence tells you which assumption fits your country, narrow the range accordingly. For example, when community maternal mortality is believed to be 1.5 to 2 times facility mortality, the plausible completeness range is narrower.

Completeness of facility maternal death reporting

Completeness relies on the UN mortality estimates. Use the built-in country data, or upload your own in the Upload Data step of Getting started.

sections.heading: Common pitfalls
sections.text:
- Treating institutional mortality as population mortality. Facilities capture only part of deaths.
- Comparing regions with very different shares of institutional births.
- Ignoring completeness. A low completeness means the reported rate is a lower bound.

ai.summary: The Mortality pages look at deaths recorded in health facilities: institutional maternal mortality, stillbirths and neonatal deaths before discharge. Institutional Mortality shows rates and plausibility checks, Mortality Mapping maps them, Mortality Completeness estimates how completely deaths are reported. Mortality uses reported deaths without the reporting-rate and outlier adjustment applied to other indicators, but still depends on the selected denominator.

Institutional mortality is not population mortality; a low completeness makes the reported rate a lower bound (#common-pitfalls)
The method, definitions and formulas are in Mortality (/en/docs/framework/9-mortality/)
